## Our Purpose
Washington, DC has spent years expanding Capital Bikeshare and its bike lane network, and DDOT's planning documents explicitly weigh ridership and revenue against equity and access when planning bikeshare expansion. Yet it remains unclear whether access to these transportation resources differs systematically across neighborhoods. This project asks: **How do a neighborhood's income, population, and bike infrastructure relate to its access to Capital Bikeshare and how much people ride? How well can these factors predict ridership in the coming month?** Throughout, we use 2020 census tracts as our operational definition of "neighborhoods."

By linking Capital Bikeshare trip records from January 2024 through October 2026, station locations built from those records and checked against DC Open Data, OpenStreetMap bike lane snapshots, ACS 5-year tract-level estimates, and LEHD LODES workplace job counts, we examine (1) whether lower-income tracts have less access to bikeshare stations and bike lanes, and (2) how well ridership in the coming month can be predicted from infrastructure and neighborhood characteristics, and where observed ridership falls short of that prediction.

The findings could help the District Department of Transportation identify potential gaps in bikeshare accessibility and evaluate where additional bicycle infrastructure or shared mobility services may be needed. By distinguishing observed ridership from infrastructure accessibility, the project seeks to inform more equitable transportation planning and public infrastructure investment decisions.

## Data-sources
We plan to integrate five data sources. 

First, Capital Bikeshare Trip History provides individual bicycle trip records from January 2024 through October 2026, including trip timestamps, geographic coordinates, and membership types.

Second, station locations are built from the trip records themselves, giving the stations in use in each month. The current station list and dock counts come from Capital Bikeshare Locations on DC Open Data, which republishes the system's GBFS feed, and are used to check the trip-based list.

Third, bicycle lanes come from OpenStreetMap extracts (Geofabrik) dated January 1 of each year, grouped into three types: separated from cars, painted lanes, and shared lanes. The DDOT Bicycle Lanes layer is used to check how complete the OpenStreetMap coverage is. 

Fourth, the American Community Survey (ACS) 5-Year Estimates provide census tract-level socioeconomic characteristics, including median household income and population. For each target month we use the newest release published before that month: the 2018–2022 release for November and December 2024, the 2019–2023 release through January 2026, and the 2020–2024 release from February 2026 on."

Fifth, LEHD LODES Workplace Area Characteristics provide job counts by census block, which we aggregate to tracts as jobs per square mile. We use the 2022 release for target months through December 2025 and the 2023 release, published December 18, 2025, from January 2026 on.

Finally, [Census Tract Boundaries](https://walker-data.com/tidycensus/articles/spatial-data.html) will be obtained using the `tidycensus` package to geographically integrate the datasets.

## Methodology
Our unit of analysis is the 2020 census tract. We build the data in R with the sf package as a tract-month panel: each trip is assigned to the tract containing its start coordinates, giving one row per tract per target month, November 2024 to November 2026 (206 × 25 = 5,150 rows). The outcome is log(1 + trip starts). Every input uses only information available before the target month. Months split into training (November 2024 to October 2025), test (November 2025 to October 2026), and a forecast month (November 2026) whose trips are not yet published.

Each row carries four kinds of inputs. Station access comes from the stations in use in the previous month: station count, stations per square mile, and distance from the tract centroid to the nearest station, with stations just outside DC kept so border tracts are not penalized. Bike lanes come from the OpenStreetMap snapshot of January 1 of the target year, in miles per square mile for separated, painted, and shared facilities, with all measurement in EPSG:2248. Neighborhood characteristics come from the ACS release in force for that month: median household income, population density, the share of households without a vehicle, bike and transit commute shares, racial composition, and median age. Workplace demand is jobs per square mile from LODES.

For RQ1, we group tracts into income quintiles and compare station density, distance to the nearest station, and bike-lane density across quintiles, using maps and summary tables. For RQ2, we tune a LASSO and a random forest with time-based cross-validation on the training months in tidymodels, run the chosen model once on the test months, and compare it with two baselines: the same as last month, and the same as the same month last year. We also fit the same model without the past-ridership inputs; where the ridership it expects exceeds actual ridership, use falls short of what a tract's infrastructure and residents predict. We compare test errors across income quintiles, and test residuals for spatial autocorrelation using Moran's I.

Three analytic decisions run through the work. We use trip starts rather than trip ends, because starts show where riders enter the system; trip ends serve as a robustness check. Very low-population tracts, such as the National Mall, are flagged, and models are reported with and without them. Dockless e-bike trips are included only if their coordinates are precise enough to place them in a tract, and missing values are imputed inside each cross-validation fold and flagged.

## Technical hurdles
We anticipate three main technical challenges. First, spatial integration and computational efficiency will require linking large volumes of trip-level coordinates, bikeshare station locations, bicycle lane geometries, and census tract boundaries using consistent coordinate reference systems. We will also need to account for bicycle lane segments crossing tract boundaries and stations located near DC's borders. To manage computational demands, we plan to aggregate spatially matched trips at the census tract level and cache intermediate results.

Second, temporal alignment may affect comparability across datasets. Capital Bikeshare trip records cover January through March 2024, while MWCOG's station and bicycle infrastructure data represent January 2024 conditions, and ACS estimates reflect socioeconomic characteristics from 2019 to 2023. Infrastructure changes during the study period and seasonal variation in ridership may influence our findings, limiting their generalizability to other months.

Third, missing and incomplete data may complicate the analysis. Some bikeshare trips lack station identifiers, potentially including dockless e-bike trips, while some ACS income estimates are missing or have substantial margins of error. Additionally, missing bicycle lane attributes may indicate inapplicable facility types rather than incomplete reporting. We will examine missingness patterns, document data-cleaning and classification decisions, and use available geographic coordinates where appropriate. We will interpret observed relationships as associations rather than causal effects.
